# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

value.markup:
MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to the tools, data and services they need. It gives every assistant the same plug, so a tool only has to be built once.

Before MCP, every AI app needed its own custom integration for every system. Want your assistant to read files, query a database or open a ticket? That meant bespoke glue code for each pairing, and it broke whenever either side changed.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to the tools, data and services they need. It gives every assistant the same plug, so a tool only has to be built once.

Before MCP, every AI app needed its own custom integration for every system. Want your assistant to read files, query a database or open a ticket? That meant bespoke glue code for each pairing, and it broke whenever either side changed.

Most AI conversations start the same way: someone copies a ticket, a log file or a chunk of code into a chat window and hopes the assistant has enough context to help.

MCP removes the copy-paste step. The assistant reads the ticket, the log or the repository directly through an MCP server, so its answer is based on real, current data.

value.markup:
With MCP, the work is split cleanly. A tool owner exposes capabilities through an MCP server. An AI client connects to that server and discovers what it can do. Either side can change without the other breaking.

The result is a growing library of tools that any compatible assistant can use, with the same permissions and the same boundaries every time.

With MCP, the work is split cleanly. A tool owner exposes capabilities through an MCP server. An AI client connects to that server and discovers what it can do. Either side can change without the other breaking.

The result is a growing library of tools that any compatible assistant can use, with the same permissions and the same boundaries every time.

For teams, that means fewer stale copies of information and fewer mistakes from outdated context. Everyone asks the same tools the same questions and gets the same answers.

It also keeps people in control. Access is granted per server, so you decide which systems an assistant can see and what it is allowed to change.

content.text:
The blog is built and running. The front page and both posts return 200 and render every block.

**What I built**
- **Schema (umbraco):** Three block element types in Blocks: Text Block (rich text), Image Block (photo and caption) and Quote Block (quote and attribution). A "Blog Body Blocks" block grid that allows those three. Two page types in Pages: Blog Front Page (title, intro, body) and Blog Post (title, date, excerpt, listing image, body). Each has its template. Site Root allows the front page, and the front page allows posts. I read each one back to confirm it saved.
- **Media:** A "Blog" folder with four photos from `unsplash/`: usb-cables, connected-structure, puzzle-hands and network-lines-dots.
- **Content (umbraco-editor):** A front page "Blog" under WWW, with two posts under it.
  - *Why MCP Is Awesome: One Plug for Every AI Tool* (1 Oct 2026): five blocks, including an image.
  - *Why MCP Is Awesome for Teams: Context Instead of Copy-Paste* (5 Oct 2026): five blocks, including an image.
  - All three pages are published, and `get-page` shows their values.
- **Domain:** The front page is assigned `/`.
- **Views:** `frontPage.cshtml` lists posts newest first, with the listing image, date, title and excerpt. `blogPost.cshtml` shows the post and its body. A shared `_Layout.cshtml` provides the page chrome. Each block has an adapter in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/`, a ViewComponent in `ViewComponents/`, and a view in `Views/Shared/Components/`. Plain models are in `Models/Blocks/`.

**How to view**
- Front page: https://localhost:44317/ (accept the self-signed certificate warning)
- Posts: https://localhost:44317/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-plug-for-every-ai-tool/ and https://localhost:44317/why-mcp-is-awesome-for-teams-context-instead-of-copy-paste/
- Backoffice: https://localhost:44317/umbraco (admin@example.com / 1234567890)
- Umbraco is running in the background (task `buya0ca08`). Stop it with TaskStop or Ctrl+C in its console.

**Checks I ran**
- `dotnet build` succeeded with 0 errors and 0 warnings, both before and after the view changes.
- `npm run build` succeeded. I confirmed Tailwind output includes the classes used in the views.
- `/` and both posts return 200. Each post renders five grid items, one image and one blockquote. None of the three pages contains "Could not render component".
- The four image URLs return 200.
- Not checked: how the page looks in a browser. I only verified the HTML and HTTP responses.

**Conflict with AGENTS.md**
- AGENTS.md shows `@await Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync(Model, "blocks")`. That fails at runtime with "The partial view 'blockgrid/blocks' was not found", and every page returns 500. The second argument is the grid view name, so I used `"default"`, which resolves to `Views/Partials/blockgrid/default.cshtml`. This keeps Umbraco's own renderer and the local grid partials. I did not edit AGENTS.md, so the example still needs correcting.

**Other notes**
- No MCP call failed. The 500 came from my view, not from the MCP servers.
- The post captions credit the photographers, as the unsplash README asks.
